title: GroundTruth: what the ground knows about the week
note: The one source for both decks: the live deck (site/talk/) reads it, and presentation/story/build_pptx.cjs builds the PowerPoint from it. Numbers are never typed here: a static slide names a chart, and talk.js draws its numbers from data/*.json (written by src/presentation_data.py). Clip cuts (start/end, seconds) are applied by src/talk_build.py.

beats.title: You shook the ground today
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Every one of you shook the ground on the way here. By car, by bus, on foot. A few billionths of a metre, but you did. And somewhere under this city, an instrument wrote it down. Here's one day of that writing.

beats.title: Weekday or weekend?
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: One whole day under Brussels, midnight to midnight. Look at the morning. Weekday, or weekend? (one beat, don't wait) It was a Wednesday: Christmas Day, 2019. Our model said Sunday. In a few minutes you'll see why it was right to be wrong.

beats.title: Last time: one question
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Two months ago we asked one question: can a seismometer tell what day it is? We made five promises. Short answer: we kept all five, then kept going. So, what is it actually hearing?

beats.title: What a seismometer records
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Every car, bus and footstep pushes on the ground and sends a tiny wave down through the rock. A seismometer is a weight on a spring: the ground moves, the weight lags, and it measures the difference. Seismologists built these for earthquakes, and everything else they call noise. This is an ordinary Wednesday in January 2020 under Brussels: quiet at night, a jump at seven, high all day. The noise is a city waking up. Aradhya, where does it come from?

beats.title: Seismometers on six continents
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: A 2020 Science paper by Lecocq and colleagues published 158 seismometers on six continents, one reading every fifteen minutes, late 2019 to mid-2020. (touch Brussels) Brussels is this one, in Uccle. Which days are weekends comes from each country's calendar, never from the shaking. Holidays and lockdown are set aside. That leaves 17,027 ordinary days to learn from.

beats.title: Two kinds of shaking
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Not all shaking is us. The slow wobbles, one every few seconds, are the ocean, waves hitting coasts hundreds of kilometres away. The fast ones, several a second, are engines, wheels and feet.

beats.title: The sea keeps no office hours
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.source: R12 data, Brussels (BE.UCC), Oct 2025 – Sep 2026, EarthScope MUSTANG
beats.notes: Held still. Left, the ocean: 11 a.m. and 3 a.m. are almost the same line; the sea doesn't keep office hours. Right, 4 to 14 hertz: daytime is about forty times stronger than night. That gap is us, so that's the band we listen to.

beats.title: Only the people band reads the week
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: And we tested it. Same model, same days, five bands. The ocean band reads weekday vs weekend 51% of the time: a coin toss. The people band: almost 99%. Shraddha, how does a model listen?

beats.title: One day becomes 25 numbers
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: A model can't look at a picture, so each day becomes 25 numbers. Twenty-four say when the city was busy, hour by hour: the shape. One says how loud the whole day was compared with that station's usual day: the level. We split them because every station is different, some next to a motorway, some in a basement. The shape is what makes cities comparable.

beats.title: A hundred trees vote
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: The model is a random forest: a hundred decision trees, each asking a few yes/no questions. A real one from Brussels: at six in the morning, was the ground still no busier than the rest of the day? Yes leads to weekend. On a Wednesday it never saw, 97 of 100 trees say weekday, but they split on which weekday.

beats.title: Graded only on weeks it never saw
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: One rule: we never grade it on a week it studied. Monday and Tuesday are near-twins, so we hide whole weeks, five rounds. And we score it so that always guessing weekday gets 50, not five out of seven: balanced accuracy. A coin toss is the floor. Aadit, how did it do?

beats.title: It reads the day
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: One forest per seismometer. Weekday or weekend: 95% in a typical city. The exact day: 47%, where guessing gets 14. In three of the emptiest places in the data, a mountain, the Kalahari, the tip of Chile, it's near chance. No people, no rhythm. And the shape matters: loudness alone names the exact day 30% of the time; with the shape, 47%.

beats.title: Its mistakes find holidays
beats.speaker: Aradhya, Aadit
beats.notes: [Aradhya] Back to Christmas: a Wednesday it had never seen, and it said Sunday, and so did the models at 71% of seismometers. On weekday holidays it never saw, it said weekend 76% of the time; on ordinary weekdays, 5%. It learned how people behave, not the calendar. [Aadit] So we turned its surprise into an alarm. Rank every day by how surprised it was, and the holidays float to the top, beating the standard alarm at 110 of 147 seismometers. We never built a holiday detector. We taught it normal.

beats.title: It recognises rest, not the name of the day
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: A model trained on all the other cities still reads a new one: 83%. Trained only on Saturday-Sunday countries, it calls Salfit's Fridays weekend: it recognises rest, not the name of the day. Jeddah, our third Friday city, didn't transfer. And when the UAE moved its weekend in 2022, we wrote the prediction down before downloading anything: Sundays got 20% quieter, luck would do that about 3 times in 1,000. One sensor, 90 km from Sharjah, and Fridays got busier, which we didn't predict.

beats.title: The dare, done properly
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.source: Result 19 (docs/17) and the second-by-second test (docs/20), both written down before running
beats.notes: Last time's dare: if we know what a city sounds like at eight on a Tuesday, can we subtract the people and find small earthquakes underneath? On fifteen-minute averages: not supported, p = 0.053, and outside one Puerto Rico swarm a simple rolling median did best. A quake lasts seconds; fifteen minutes blurs it away. So we wrote a proper test down in advance: second-by-second recordings, years the first test never touched, at most 100 quakes per station so no swarm decides it. (read the result card) Detecting quakes that happened; never predicting them. Shraddha, what else didn't work?

beats.title: What didn't work
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: Three honest ones. Lockdown didn't make weekdays look like Sundays: only about a quarter were called weekend; it looked like no day the model had heard. Our shape-plus-level split doesn't beat raw hourly numbers; it's about as good, and easier to compare. And all of this is one season, with national holidays only. So: what happens with years?

beats.title: Now scale it
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Results 15–17, Jan 2019 – Sep 2026, 33 cities, EarthScope MUSTANG
beats.notes: We went back to the source: seven years, every station from the study that is still recording and publicly served, plus Sharjah. 33 cities, 72,000 ordinary days. This is a new, bigger model: three frequency bands, every half hour, gradient boosting, still tested only on weeks it never saw. A new experiment, so new numbers.

beats.title: More data helps, then flattens
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: Results 16–18, 2019–26, 33 cities, every score on weeks the model never saw
beats.notes: The obvious bet: seven years makes it much smarter. Weekend or not: 97%. But the exact day climbs from 38% at 100 days to 57% with all of them, and flattens. One model for all 33 cities together: worse in every city. A Tuesday just sounds like a Thursday. Show it the week around the day instead: 96%.

beats.title: Ask the ground
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: This is all of it, live: 33 cities, any day from 2019 to last September. (Brussels, Christmas 2019) From the day alone: Sunday, sure of it. From the week around it: Wednesday, sure of it. A Wednesday that looked like a day off. (Next: the globe on Monday 23 March 2020) And this is the week the world stopped. (two seconds) Of the 24 cities we measure clearly, 12 were at least 15% quieter than their normal that Monday; a week later, 17. Nobody told the globe there was a pandemic.

beats.title: A test running every night
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: City Pulse, pre-registered in docs/19, interim
beats.notes: And it doesn't stop in September. Every night this page downloads yesterday for seven cities and guesses the day before it's told. This term we added a second model that also learns each ordinary day once it has been graded. Does learning help? We wrote the test down before writing the code, and our own guess is probably not much, because more data already flattened. The verdict comes in January; until then these numbers say interim.

beats.title: Five promises, kept
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: (no read-out: let it sit while you walk to the centre, then Next)

beats.title: Still useless?
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: So: seismometers. Still useless? There's a network already buried under many of the world's cities, recording for decades, free. It hears a neighbourhood, not a person: no phones, no cameras. And ours is running tonight. Everyone measures how loud the ground is. We taught a model what normal sounds like, and its mistakes tell us when something happened. That's GroundTruth. Thank you.

beats.title: Backup: does it remember what it studied?
beats.speaker: Q&A
beats.notes: Same 7-year models: days it trained on vs weeks it never saw. The gap is memorisation, which is why every number in this talk is on unseen weeks.

beats.title: Backup: running live
beats.speaker: Q&A
beats.notes: Every night the website scores the latest days, about two days behind, with models that never saw them.
